A cellar below the Silver Road Counting-House keeps a second set of books, for the Binder trade the Sharp Hands profit from. (test assumption: faction-places.md's secret hook for the Counting-House, used as the sub-faction's own hidden side; canon says the Sharp Hands 'barely have a private side')
They fear a crackdown: the old powers uniting to crush them before they're strong enough.
Some priests are sincere and ashamed; they are its likeliest reformers.
Their warmth to their own: once counted as theirs, you're protected like family.
Many run goods for the Night Market.
Many Binders don't like what they do, but see it as their only way of being accepted.
Almost every Warden lost someone to the green; the jokes keep the grief down.
They guard the Womb of Creation.
In one night every mule team the Saltmarket hauling crews own, thirty-two head, was taken from the quay stables. With nothing to haul it, the season's salt is piling up on the New Quay.

Dorog Coin-counter's Counting-House bought the Saltmarket crews' quay loan from the Open Council's harbour bank and called it in before term. The crews' carts, harness and sheds stand forfeit, and Saltmarket salt now leaves only on Counting-House carts.

Counting-House factors have bought the carrying debts of the salt crews on every road and sea-lane out of the coast, and sell salt only for Counting-House notes, at three times last year's price. From Oathford to the Elder Vale to the Wide Bay, salt is dear before the curing season.

The Counting-House now lends salt against pledges: furs, rations, swords and labour. Where a pledge falls due unpaid, its factors take the pledge, and the pledger is bonded to work off the rest. The foothill clans, the Green Wall and the Broken Rim have all been offered salt on these terms.

Kodor Debt-taker has called in the salt notes at Wainyard, Bogford and Shellring. The Counting-House now owns the shops, fields and boats pledged there, and every defaulter who could not pay has been marched off in debt-bond, 'to work it off at the Counting-House'.

On Dorog Coin-counter's sworn complaint, the harbour courts at Saltmarket and Openharbour have named Brisa Tolland a cheat who sold the crews' salt short and kept the quay dues, together with her tally-clerk Corwen Abbot. Open Hand markets on the harbour coast bar them both, and no one may take salt under their tally-mark.

Dorog's men have taken the New Quay under forfeit and sealed the Road Crews' salt sheds from Saltmarket to the Silver Road. The crews who barred the sheds against them are held under debt-writ in the Counting-House's lower yard.

Dorog Coin-counter had the Saltmarket teams taken so that the crews would default on the quay loan he had already bought; and every debtor his salt notes break is entered in a second set of books in the cellar under the Counting-House, and sold on to the Binders at the Chainmarket.
Anselm Crake signs every Saltmarket note for the Counting-House and answers for them to Dorog Coin-counter himself.
Counting-House salt notes carry a bond clause: a note that can't be redeemed in coin is owed in labour, to the Counting-House, at the Counting-House's rate.

The Far Sails will carry salt by sea for any town or crew that breaks with the Counting-House notes, if those they carry for swear never to give a runaway's name to anyone who asks, and give the fleet free berth wherever they load.
Quenna Ashby, keeper of the Counting-House day-books and a freed bondswoman, refused to enter salt pledges taken in labour, and Dorog Coin-counter took the day-books out of her hands.
Every salt-boat licence on the Saltmarket bar this season was bought in one lot, in the spring, by the Sharp Hands' Saltmarket counting-room.

Pruett Lisle, the night stable-keeper, unbarred the yard from inside with the stable key and let the teams be driven off up the cove track; he was paid for it, and glad of the chance to hurt the crews who threw him off the teams last spring.
Varga Holm spent the night of the theft in the reeve's lock-up for brawling at the salt-row alehouse; the reeve's book shows it.
Ulla Brenn raised the alarm, and the yard bolt was drawn from the inside with the stable key, which she has never held.
The crews blame Varga Holm, who offered to buy the teams cheap a month ago and was turned away loudly; they mean to run him out of Saltmarket by week's end.
The salt is the crews' own and lawful to sell at Openharbour; only the bar licence stands in the way, and no licence is to be had this season.
Varga is innocent of the theft: the reeve's own book has him in this lock-up the night the teams went.
Varga Holm, freed, will say before any arbiter that he drove Saltmarket salt to the Openharbour Salt Steps for the crews for eleven years, and always sold it from the bottom three steps.

At Openharbour the Salt Steps sellers can buy only Counting-House salt, at Counting-House prices, and the carters who still bring Saltmarket salt in by the coast road are being robbed before they reach the gate.
Crail Hennock's band are carters who lost their carrying work on the coast road when the Counting-House carts took it; they were driven off the Saltmarket road and now live in the lime kilns.
Why here: driven out. Crail Hennock's band were driven off the coast road's carrying work, and now take the only salt still moving on it: the independent carters' loads bound for the Salt Steps.
The harbour council has already voted to move the salt market off the Steps into the new salt hall next spring; the pitch will be worth nothing to either side.
The Saltmarket crews have sold from the bottom three steps since the stair was cut; no grant gives them the right, only use, and the forfeit papers never mention the Steps at all.

The Saltmarket crews' forfeit carts and harness have been driven up to Carter's Rest to be sold under the Counting-House's writ, and the Long Shed is splitting over whether the Road Crews strike against Sharp Hands rates before the Counting-House buys their notes too.

Cause: a side taken in someone else's quarrel. Elric bought two of the Saltmarket crews' forfeit carts at the Counting-House writ-sale, which Cador calls taking the Sharp Hands' side against the Saltmarket crews.
Guilty: Dace drove two of the crews' forfeit carts out of the Counting-House yard by night. The forfeit was lawful under the loan, and he did take them.

At Oathford the lord's toll-steward passes Counting-House salt carts toll-free and doubles the toll on every other salt load, and the river town's eel-smokers, who cure the whole catch in salt, can now buy only note-salt.
Teague's mule never left the far bank that night; the Oathford ferryman saw it tethered there till dawn.

Corin Lusk, Ivo's uncle, met the boy on the reed path, took the row's pooled salt-coin from him and sent him upriver to a cousin, because the toll-steward's men had his name for toll-dodging. Corin used the coin to pay the doubled toll on his own boat. Motive: preservation.
Why here: opportunity. With salt at three times last year's price, the row's salt-houses are the richest thing on the river and nobody guards them.
Wendel Coyle sold Harl's band the night the row's note-salt came in, for a share, because the row docked his pay to buy it.
Innocent: the doubled salt toll was never set by the lord. Gideon set it himself, under a warrant whose imperial seal is forged, and Wilda paid every lawful toll on the salt she brought upriver.
Elderhollow's old houses refuse Counting-House notes, so no salt is coming in at all; the winter barrels can't be put down, and the Low Shrine's kitchen has begun rationing its soup.
Hamund Lowry, Elderhollow's salt-buyer, was found drowned at the Elder ford with the houses' pooled salt-coin gone.
No crime: Hamund drowned crossing the ford in spate, rather than wait a day for the ferry; the purse went downstream with the current.
Kesh crossed the ford a day after Hamund drowned, by the ferryman's own tally.
The outer ring blames Kesh Arlow, the Qotiro pedlar seen at the ford, for Hamund's death.
Innocent: Kesh bought his salt for coin at Saltmarket before the notes; the paper found on him is a Saltmarket receipt, not a Counting-House note.
Why here: paid. Anselm Crake pays Rudd Calloway's band to rob every salt-run Elderhollow sends out, so the town takes the notes or goes without.
Edda Rowe tells Rudd's band when the Low Shrine's salt-runs leave; they pay her in salt, and it all goes into the soup.

With the coast's salt under notes, the Far Sails have begun running salt by sea, bought off the boilers' pans at night, to towns that refuse the notes; the fleet's own stores went short to do it, and the skerry huts are curing their catch on half the salt it needs.
Source: spoiled stores. The victualler's curing house salted the autumn catch thin to free salt for the sea-runs, and the half-cured fish is making the huts sick. Careless, not deliberate.
Paid: Halvard worked his passage off on Sorcha's own salt-runs this summer; her mate kept the tally and can swear to it.
Ronan Merle's salt boat went down under the Lantern Rock with the coast's salt aboard; he drowned.

Fitch Garvey, Ronan's deckhand and Anselm Crake's informer, holed the boat so the run would fail, to keep his own family off the Counting-House's bond-roll as he had been promised. Motive: preservation.
Sorcha was on the Raft for the captains' vote the night Ronan's boat sailed.
Ronan Merle left his salt-run share to the skerry huts' widows' kettle, and Captain Ione Brask still holds it.

At the Foothill post the acting trade-elder has pledged the clans' coming winter furs to the Counting-House for salt, and trappers who won't trade through him can't cure their hides: half the valley's catch is spoiling in the pits.
The surveyor spent the night the brine was fouled at the Gap pass hut, under guest-right, in front of six clansmen.
Torvin, Hild's own son, fouled the brine pits with tallow so the trappers would have to cure through the trade-hall; the acting elder paid him in lowland coin. Motive: greed.
Elin Ridgeway is pledged to work a season at the Counting-House fur-store for her family's salt.
The High Snows will not take in a girl pledged to the Counting-House: sheltering a pledge-breaker would bring writ-men up the pass, and the hold has never let lowland law climb the snowline.
Aldwin Scree, the Foothill post's old trade-elder, died at the turn of autumn.
The trade-hall's fur rights are pledged to the Counting-House through the winter; whoever wins the hall inherits the pledge with it.
Aldwin meant the hall for Mairead and told his old guide-companion so; Cullen kept the old man's furs in trust and pledged them to the Counting-House the day after the burial.

The Counting-House offered the Green Wall a winter's salt for its rations against a pledge of the wall's salvage rights in the lost villages; Haʻo refused, and the wall's winter meat is hanging unsalted while the patrols go short.

Haʻo of the Green Wall and Silas Crewe swore before the wall that a shooting match between the wall's archers and the factor's cart-guards will decide the winter's salt: at the old coin price if the wall wins, on pledge of the salvage rights if the guards win.
Fix type: bought judge. Silas has paid off Noll Haskett, one of the two line-judges, through his Firststone debts.
Haʻo has promised Kit Ambrey that if he wins the match he may leave the wall and go home; the wall cannot spare a single bow, and Haʻo knows it.
Innocent: Dunstan carried the factor's pledge-letter in the open, at his quartermaster's order, and never knew Haʻo had refused the pledge.
Hidden motive (put them there): Osgar asked the factor for the pledge-letter himself and gave it to Dunstan to carry; he wants the boy out before anyone asks who sent him.

Wynn Halloran was killed at the Green Wall's gate by Rorik Vane, captain of the Counting-House cart-guards, when the wall turned the salt carts back; Garoṭaqa's court at Firststone acquitted Rorik for lack of proof.
The wall's gate-boy saw Rorik draw first on an unarmed man; Rorik had Kodor Debt-taker's order to bring the carts through the gate 'or not come back paid'.
Tegan Marlow's younger brother Hal pledged his own labour for a sack of salt for the wall's cookhouse, and the Counting-House holds him at its foothill wagon-yard.

Ironstep's young warriors have taken the Counting-House's salt in pledge of their swords and ride as its salt-cart guards; the lowland villages along the carts' road now blame the Last Wave for the notes, and the enclave's elders fear the young are buying a war with Ironstep's winter.
The step-hall elders and the Counting-House hiring-master swore in the duel circle that bouts there decide which Ironstep warriors the Counting-House may hire for its carts.
Fix type: loaded gear. Bastian gave the hotheads weighted practice-staves and the steady fighters split ones, so only the young who want war win places on the carts.
Hew Garside's band took Teo Brandt for his skill: they need a farrier to shoe the Counting-House cart-horses they've been stealing off the road.
Hidden motive (revenge on the captor): Kael wants Hew's band dead for his horse and his pride, and will reject any way that leaves them breathing.
The riders' winter pay-salt is held under seal in the Counting-House salt-vault until a ruling on a salt cart the riders lost on the road.
The lost cart was taken by Hew Garside's band, not lost by the riders; the contract's ruling would clear them, but the hearing has been put off twice.
A lowland herdsman, Osmund Teale, has challenged Kael Dunmore on blood terms in the Ironstep duel circle, for a brother the cart-guards beat on the road.

Wainyard took salt on notes all last winter; Kodor Debt-taker called them in, and now the Counting-House owns the cart-sheds and the freed families' shops, and a third of the village has been marched off in debt-bond.
Nat Bewley was on the road to Carter's Rest with the Wainyard post-cart that night; the Long Shed's yard book has him.

Jory Venn sawed the shed's roof-tree to bring the roof down on the factor's tally-room and its debt-books; it fell the other way, onto the grain store the village still eats from. Motive: desperation.
Source: spoiled stores. With the roof down and no salt or hands to turn it, the seized grain has gone to black mould; the bread made from it is sickening the children.

Lida Kestrel read the salt notes aloud to Wainyard's households and vouched for them; the bond clause was written into the notes in Counting-House cipher, and when Kodor called them in, the village lost its shops and Lida's son was marched off with the rest. Magistrate Ladd upheld every note.
Kodor wrote the cipher clause himself; Ladd upheld the notes because his own debts are held at the Counting-House.

Bogford's grain fields were pledged against salt notes; Kodor called them in, the Counting-House owns the fields now, and the men who worked them were marched off in debt-bond, leaving the women and old folk to bring in a harvest that is no longer theirs.
Gorse Abney's reivers took Rhea Dunlin to silence her: she saw them stripping the houses of the men who were marched off, and knows their faces.

Cause: a side taken. Nan's husband took the field-reeve's post over the seized fields. The break protects Nan's children: the reeve's household stays off the bond-roll only while it is seen to stand apart from the village.
Kodor Debt-taker keeps a pack of bond-mastiffs on the pledged fields; they are Counting-House property under its warrant, and killing one is theft from the Counting-House.
The hounds come through where the field-reeve had the old hedge grubbed out to plough to the common's edge; the fence was never mended.

Shellring's boats were pledged against salt notes; Kodor called them in, the Counting-House sold the boats at Reefhold, and the families who couldn't pay were marched off in debt-bond. The village that is left keeps the reef's old house-records and little else.
Why here: opportunity. With the boats sold and the young men bonded, Shellring has nothing to stop a crew from the wreckers' cove taking what's on the racks.
Emrys Kettle died a week after the boats were taken; his last skiff was beached for caulking and the Counting-House missed it.
Emrys told the whole stump-ring the skiff was 'for whoever keeps fishing'; he never named an heir.
The Shellring house-roll, which lists every family and line on the reef, was pledged against the village's salt notes and forfeit to Kodor Debt-taker with the boats.
The roll is the Counting-House's proof of every Shellring debt-line; Kodor keeps it because every bonded name on it can be followed.

At Openharbour the ruling has turned the market against Brisa's crews: buyers won't touch salt that ever passed her tally, haulers who carried under her mark are being dunned for the salt the harbour impounded, and the crews' first-wagon place at the salt fair is up for grabs.

Rhosyn Tarrow, for the crews, and Garth Mowbray, for the Counting-House, swore at the fair-stone to abide the fair's old custom: when a holder is disgraced, the first-wagon place goes to the winner of the hauling race.
Inflated: Orla counts the impounded salt at fair-day price, not the price she paid Ned, and has added the harbour's impound fee twice.
Cause: false, spread by someone off the card. Brisa sold every load at full weight; the complaint was sworn elsewhere and repeated here.
Ysmay Corran, the harbour market-warden, kept the Salt Steps' weigh-book and never was asked for it by the court.

In Saltmarket the ruling stands in the crews' own town: no quay will load salt under Brisa's mark, her tally-clerk Corwen Abbot is barred with her, and the crews who stood by her are being made to choose.
Doruḍoqu will not take a clerk under the harbour ban into the Long Shed: the Sharp Hands would bar the Road Crews' own tallies the next day.
By Saltmarket custom, when a quaymaster is disgraced the tally-staff goes by a bout in the crews' bout-ring at the quay's end; Sabine Cotter and Royce Hendry have sworn to abide it.
After the ruling, Brisa called Anselm Crake a liar and a forger before the whole quay and threw his tally-board into the harbour.
Brisa said exactly that, and the crowd heard every word; she said nothing about the theft of the teams.

The Counting-House holds the coast's salt road: the New Quay is sealed, the crews' sheds are shut from Saltmarket to the Silver Road, and the crews who barred them sit in the lower yard under debt-writ.
The salt is the Road Crews' own and was never part of the Saltmarket loan; the gate turns it back only because it has no Counting-House note.
Innocent: the sealed sheds were Road Crews property and owed nothing under the Saltmarket loan; the writ that holds the crews names debts they never signed.
Hidden motive (wants the credit): Elric means to bring the crews home himself, to stand on Cador's side of the Long Shed again as the man who freed them.
Dorog Coin-counter swore the false complaint that named Brisa Tolland a cheat and barred her from every market on the harbour coast, and his men took her quay.
Every word of the revelation holds; the second books are in the cellar under this hall, and Dorog keeps the cellar key on his own chain.
In Saltmarket the New Quay stands sealed under the Counting-House's forfeit; the crews have no quay, no carts and no teams, and the salt-boilers are selling to whoever will fetch their salt.

Mott Selby went after the crews' tally-box the night the quay was sealed, to burn his own debts to the crews; he took Hanne for Joss in the dark, and she ran with the box and is hiding in the old salt cellars. Motive: desperation.
Royce was in the Counting-House tally-room at Saltmarket with Anselm's clerks all night, sealing the forfeit papers.
Cause: deliberately ruined. The crews' hauling was ruined on purpose, as the record of the stolen teams shows; who did it is not on this card.
The skerry huts' oar-crew will meet the crews' salt with their skiffs where the Silver Road comes down to the sea.

Morwen Scarth, for the widows' kettle, and Captain Ione Brask swore on the Raft to let the oar-race round the skerries decide whether Ronan Merle's share goes to the kettle or back into the salt-runs.
Inflated: the yard values the sack at the Counting-House's winter price and charges Hal his own board.
Hal Fother, out of the wagon-yard, can draw the watch-rounds of the Counting-House's lower yard, where he was kept a week before they sent him up the foothill road.
Hidden motive (needs the captive's support back): Tegan's cook's wage doesn't feed their mother; Hal's did, and she has said nothing about the debts that are coming due.
Counting-House cart-guards from Ironstep beat Osmund Teale's brother on the cart road below the Rim.
Kael Dunmore, alive, knows the cart road the bond-line takes past Bogford and will ride it with the player.
Elsbet Crane will stand before the Open Council and tell how Bogford's men were marched off on the bond-line.
Ivar Coltrane, the Counting-House field-reeve, struck Elsbet Crane from the gleaners' roll after the hounds quarrel, so her children may not glean the fields their father ploughed.
Ewan Marr, crewing a Tide House kelp boat, can carry the Saltmarket crews' tallies by sea around the ban-gates.
Ewan Marr and a Reefhold diver swore before the dive-master to let a deep dive decide who takes the open kelp-boat berth.
Wharf-master Ormond Vale struck Ysmay Corran from the market-warden's post for having let Brisa Tolland's salt onto the Salt Steps.
Ysmay Corran will bring the Salt Steps' weigh-book before the Open Council at the Scales Hall.
Robin Shaw, safe, will haul for the Saltmarket crews' new trade and bring three Silver Road shed-hands with him.
Cause: buyers went elsewhere. With every team gone, the crews buy no harness, and the boat-owners who carry the salt now want sea-rope the walk has never made.
Ranulf's chits are worthless: no writ-sale takes them, and he has sold forty to crew families who hoped to buy back their forfeit carts.
Hob was at the Crownsgate alehouse the whole night of the theft; half the village saw him there.
Alder Rosen, the miller's own apprentice, who keeps a key to the bridge-store, took the miller's salt-cask and sold it at the note price in Highcrossing.
Tithe-master Cuthbert Rane called in Elowen Pugh's tithe-debt a season early, against its terms, and took her salt-barrels for it now that salt is worth three times what it was.
The tithe-house is calling every salt-holding debtor early this autumn; the barrels go to the Armed Nave's stores.
Reefhold's harbour-warden has barred any salt that comes through the reef-gate without a Counting-House note.
The ban is the warden's own; the Seated Houses never asked for it.
Cause: a side taken. Torsten took the Counting-House's salt for his sword, and Aric called it selling the camp's honour to lowlanders.
Why here: opportunity. With the Green Wall's patrols cut short for want of salted rations, nobody watches Wellstone's edge, and Crow's crew take what the salvagers haul out.
Owain Tull sold Crow's crew the salvagers' haul-days for a sack of salt.
When Wainyard's notes were called, the Wainyard wheelwright who held Mabon Rill's small debt was ruined and sold it to a Chainmarket debt-broker.
Paid: Mabon paid the wheelwright off at midsummer; the receipt is with the wheelwright's widow.
Hidden motive (afraid of retaliation): Davin wants it kept quiet; if the Counting-House stables learn his brother sits in a Binder yard, he loses his place.
A Reefhold dock-thief robbed Netta of the nets' price on the stilt-walk; ashamed to go home with nothing, she is hiding in the poor stilts, mending other people's nets for food.
Hidden motive (needs the captive's support back): Alwyn's bog-iron wage is all Gwyneth would have to live on this winter; she talks only about the money.
Innocent: Alwyn was never on the Bogford debt-roll; the bailiff took him for a runaway because every other Bogford man of his age is on it.
Cedric Drewe's last delivery to the fish-row was crew salt under Brisa Tolland's barred tally-mark.
Cedric delivered full weight, as the fish-row's own weigh-slip shows; the fishmonger is right that the law now forbids her to sell it.

Seal type: held as surety for someone else's debt. Rhian bought the sacks cheap the day after the ruling, knowing what the mark meant; the clerk's seal is lawful, and her tale of buying them before is not true.

Source: spoiled stores. Saltmarket's fish-sheds cured their catch thin when their marked salt was impounded, and their headman sold the half-cured barrels off cheap to the Openharbour row to be rid of them; Agnes bought them for the row's winter. Careless, not deliberate.
Dickon Faull broke into a sealed Road Crews shed on the coast road and drove off the Prothero salt-wagon, which he sold in Openharbour.
The wagon is the Protheros' own, built by Sian's grandfather; Ottar paid a fair price for it to a man he didn't know.
Fenton struck the writ-man as he ran; the writ now names him for assault as well as the crews' debts.
The fisher families have beached at the shingle since before the New Quay was built; no grant covers it.
The Old Gate House's gate has not been closed in two hundred years.
The old houses trust the Old Hands with their quiet business: what goes through the Old Gate is never spoken of again.

Brannoc Weir, keeper of the Old Hands' cache at the Quiet Crossing, has turned the syndicate's quiet crossings into the Binders' road. On dark-moon nights Qotiro captives come over from the Marches dressed as house servants, on servant passes drawn by Absalom Quaile, who was told they were Old Gate business, and are sold to old houses that want Qotiro hands. Sevrin Locke keeps the tally and takes the houses' coin; Lord Ithiel Saxby is the best of his buyers. With the houses' work drying up, the road now pays half the syndicate's keep, in Free Lords marks. If it comes out, the buying houses are shamed before the Seated Houses, the Old Hands' name goes with them, and Absalom Quaile's hand is on every pass.

Brannoc Weir's men hold the Quiet Crossing and the cache by force. Two Old Gate runners who came to close the crossing were beaten and thrown in the river, and the crossing now runs for whoever pays Weir.

Brannoc Weir bought Absalom Quaile's debts from the Elderhollow moneylender, the arrears on his workroom and his wife's burial loan, called them in the same day, and had Kester Mold take Absalom from his workroom at Ashring in debt-bond, to work it off at the cache 'with his pen'.

At the new moon Brannoc Weir paid the Elderhollow letter-carriers' runner to carry copies of three houses' bills of sale (the Ormsby, Tarrant and Coldwell houses' purchases of Qotiro servants) to each house's rival, sealed with Absalom Quaile's own seal and naming him as their carrier. Every house on the Vale road now believes the Old Gate sold its secrets, by Absalom's hand.
Absalom Quaile draws passes and seals for Brannoc Weir's cache, and has for nine years.
The old houses have stopped sending their lineage copying to Shellring; for two seasons it has gone to the Ninth Ring archive's own scribes, and the copy-house desks stand empty.
Cause: the buyers went elsewhere. The houses moved their copying to the archive because the Shellring copies carried the Old Hands' corrections, and the houses no longer want them.
This season the Old Gate paid the Shellring copy-house's arrears in one bag of new-struck Free Lords marks.

Forty years ago Absalom Quaile forged the Carrow house's lost marriage-roll, and the house kept its seat in Elderhollow. This spring, at the stump-ring before the house-elders, Maelis Carrow acknowledged the favor and refused to repay it: 'The Carrow house owes the Old Gate nothing it will say aloud.'

Lord Ithiel Saxby stands behind Maelis Carrow's refusal because Sevrin Locke asked it of him. Saxby buys his house-servants through Sevrin; and the fewer houses that fear the Old Gate, the more the syndicate needs Weir's road.
This year Absalom Quaile has drawn a long run of house-servant passes for the cache at the Quiet Crossing, at the Old Gate's usual rate.
Since the fever year, Lady Senna Arkwright has barred Great House physicians from the Vale road; her gate turns them back at the Mount.
The Dunmere heir's fever is the river-fever the Great House surgeons have cured for twenty years; the Vale healers lose one child in three to it.
Old Nessa Thorley says the Quiet Crossing is spoken for on every dark-moon night this season, by the cache.
Sefi Ulmer was bought for the Saxby house; she knows its steward by sight, and saw Kester Mold count her over the crossing for Sevrin Locke's tally.

Arno Ure cut the Reed Ferry's rope himself, on Sevrin Locke's order: with the ferry down, every crossing on that stretch of river goes through Weir's ford. He did it to keep his father's ferry out of Weir's hands, he thinks.
Gyda Fallon was cutting reeds on the far bank with six others the night the rope parted.

Arno Ure was taken off the Reed Ferry into the crossing's service by Sevrin Locke the week Weir's men took the crossing, against the ferry indenture his father holds; he rows Weir's dark-moon boat down to the Briarlees road now.
Sevrin Locke holds Arno Ure in the cache's service against the Ure ferry indenture, and turned Wenna Ure off the landing when she came for him.
Sevrin keeps Arno because a ferryman's son can row the dark-moon boat without a light; Weir has told him to keep the boy whatever the father pays.
Sevrin Locke now keeps the Quiet Crossing's toll, which the Ure family's reed hamlet must pay to reach the Mount's market.

Baldric Ure, the reed ferryman, will stand with Absalom Quaile: forty years ago Absalom drew the charter that kept the ferry in the Ure family. His price: a new ferry rope, and the Old Gate's word that Arno is out of Weir's service for good.

When Kester Mold read the bond at the Ashring stone-milk well, Headwoman Isolde Varn held the lantern for him; Tamsin Quaile cursed her before the whole village as a house dog who held the light while they took an old man.
Isolde Varn's name in Ashring: the headwoman who keeps the village's peace with the houses.
Isolde held the lantern because Kester's bond was lawful and she feared what the cache men would do in the dark; she sent a boy to the Old Gate that night, and the Old Gate sent no one.

The bond Kester Mold read at the well was written on the Elderhollow moneylender's notes and bought by Brannoc Weir; Weir's men threw Absalom's seal-box onto the cart with his loose goods and sold them at the pilgrim stalls of the Vale wayside shrine.
Absalom's seal-box holds Brannoc Weir's written orders for a year of dark-moon passes, each marked 'set against the debt'.
Twenty years ago the Old Hands forged Cobb Ainsley's family out of their Elderhollow lease, for a house that wanted the ground.
By the cache's own hand, Absalom Quaile's debt was worked off twice over in passes: Weir's orders in the seal-box say so, line by line.
Truth: paid. Absalom's debt was worked off in passes long ago; Weir holds him because his hand is on every pass and Weir wants more.
Brannoc Weir keeps the houses' bills of sale, every Qotiro sold over the crossing with the buying house and the price, in the cache strongbox, entered in Sevrin Locke's tally hand.
Brannoc Weir, who employed Absalom Quaile for nine years, put Absalom's seal on the letters that burned the houses, so that the houses would hunt the old forger instead of the cache.
Weir means to sell to the houses directly once the Old Gate is disgraced: with the Old Hands' name gone, the houses that still want Qotiro hands will have only his road.
Under the Market Road's plain door opens only after dark.
Yaweth is planning the biggest score in the island's history; every fence on the coast knows it.
No one owns the Night Market: it has no lord, no patron and no creditor.

Yaweth is broke. Twelve years ago she bought the first cellar Under the Market Road with a loan from Mardoc Strell, a Chainmarket debt-broker, pledged against her own bond and the shop's; the last of it falls due at the autumn toll-count, and for a year she has shorted every crew's share to keep up the payments, sending the coin to the Chainmarket by Quint Ravel's hand. Her way out is the biggest score: the Great Bridge's toll-count silver, the one night a year's tolls lie in the toll-house on the span. The score is real, and Shahayuh's bridge guard hang thieves from the span: every crew she sends will die there. If it comes out, the crews walk, Strell takes Yaweth in bond and the shop with her, and the Night Market has an owner.

Yaweth has cried the Great Bridge score in every Night Market shop from Openharbour to Southroad: every crew is called to the toll-count night, and she has put it about on every quay that any crew who stays home is informing to the bridge.

Two nights after Fergus Callan stood up at the Saltmarket fence's table and called the score a gallows, the shop's share-box was lifted from the fence's cellar, and Yaweth had it dug out from under the floor of Fergus's net-loft before the whole Market. He is cried a skimmer who kept back the take, and no fence, crew or quay will deal with him.
Fergus Callan is cried a skimmer who kept back the Market's take.

On the eve of the autumn toll-count Yaweth paid Mardoc Strell his price to tear up her bond before it fell due: the year of the crews' held-back shares, the savings the dockhands keep with the shop (Fergus Callan's eleven years among them), and a tithe of the score's advance on top to make him let her go early. Strell's clerk read the payment out at the Chainmarket to clear her, and by morning every crew knew whose shares had bought Yaweth her freedom.
A bale of Far Sails pearl-shell went out of the Long Bond warehouse on a moonless night, past a locked door and a night watchman.
Tolan Greaves, the Long Bond's night watchman, let the bale out through the tide-door himself, to pay the debt-taker who holds his brother's bond.
Pim Arkle was aboard Captain Freck's boat all night, on anchor watch, and the bosun logged him.
Every Market crew on the harbour was told the same week to keep the autumn toll-count night free, and not to say why.
Wharf-master Ormond Vale has ordered the harbour watch to raid the moving market in the old Saltmarket salt-barn tonight.
The raid is real and honest: the wharf-master has had a list of the barn's stalls from a customs clerk, and means to make an example before the autumn tolls.
The strike kitchen on Haulers' Row has fed the idle crews since their mule teams were taken off the quay, and it has run out of everything but salt.
The night's float for the carters came out of the shop in Free Lords chain-marks, not harbour silver.
Last winter Radek Orlo's carts ran the hamlet's ox-cart off the toll-dodge trail into the Reeve's Ditch; the ox died and Cuthred Alby's harvest was lost with it.
Shahayuh's toll-reeves have found the mouth of the toll-dodge trail below the Great Bridge.
The hamlet's carts used the trail for forty years before the Market found it; the Market's crews widened it and made it worth finding.
A Market scout has been timing the bridge guard's changes from the trail's end every night this month.
Last spring the Ferrand reef-chart was stolen from the Ferrand pilot-hulk at Gull Landing.
Nim Sattery lifted the chart on Quint Ravel's word, and Quint fenced it at the moving market himself, off the share-book; the coin went to the Chainmarket.
The Ferrand chart is the only true chart of the Anchorage's inner reef; since it went, two Far Sails boats have holed themselves coming in.
The chart's seller wanted the price on the spot and in full, 'because the shop has a payment due at the Chainmarket'.
Why here (public): Mardoc Strell, a Chainmarket debt-broker, pays Ruck Danner's bond-takers to collect from the Saltmarket fences in kind, against a debt he says the Market owes him.
Quint Ravel, who carries the shop's coin, told Strell that the fences on Fence Row hold the Market's stock, and this season his payments came short.
Vasko Mell's men took Lenny Gallin from the lighter quay to make his mother's crew row the score's boats on the toll-count night.
Why taken: as leverage.

Hessa Lorne, the Notch boatwright who refused to caulk the score's boats, was found drowned under the hulks the night Vasko Mell's men took the boat-shed. The Market's table cleared Vasko for want of proof, and would not hear a word for a woman said to be informing.
Vasko drowned Hessa on Yaweth's word: 'see to the boatwright before she sees to the bridge'.

Hessa's tally of what the score needs (the boats, the bridge-irons, the climbing ropes) names the toll-house plan Quint Ravel bought from a Southroad bridge mason, and the hide on the toll-dodge trail where he keeps it.
The plan shows the toll-house strongroom has one way out, over the span: the bridge guard can close both ends with a whistle.

Petra Gallin, boss of a Saltmarket lighter crew, will stand with Fergus Callan, who carried her crew's first share and taught her son to swim. Her price: her crew's held-back season share paid out first, before any other crew's.
Fergus will not go because leaving is a confession: on the coast a man who runs from the Market's table is guilty.
The share-box dug from under Fergus's floor was still sealed with the Saltmarket fence's wax and had never been opened: whoever buried it never took a coin.
Cause: false, spread by someone off the card.
Fergus Callan lodged his savings with the shop under the Market Road (eleven years of shares, as dockhands do) against the day he buys a boat of his own.
Yaweth, who has employed Fergus Callan as her quay-runner for twenty years, spent his eleven years of lodged savings on her own freedom, after crying him a skimmer for the box she had lifted herself.
Yaweth still means to run the bridge, alone and with Strell's takers for a crew; she owes Strell the toll silver too.
The Wayhouse's Lending Wall is a wall of pigeonholes holding letters to and from every scholar on the road, and the letters of everyone who cannot write.

The 'forged Writers files' sold on the Night Market's stalls are real. The halls keep back a file on every family whose letters pass through the Lending Wall and the letter-writers' stalls (debts, births, quarrels, what the letters say) and use them to decide who learns what, and when. Aurel Vantry, a copyist at the Wayhouse, has been copying the held-back files for Nerys Hallam, a Night Market forger, who sells each family its own file, and anyone's file to whoever pays. If it comes out, every family that ever wrote through a letter-writer learns the Writers read and kept what they wrote; the people who cannot write lose the only post they have; and the Wayhouse loses the trust it stands on.

Nerys Hallam sold the Mount a bundle of Writers' files on its own tithe-debtors. Hotorìṭo's preachers have read lines from them in every parish shrine of the Crown Crossing, calling the Lending Wall a spy's wall, and the faithful have been told not to write through a Writers' hand.

Nerys Hallam bought the debt on the Tunstall cottage at Crownsgate, then sold Agna and Garet Tunstall the copies of Ilsa's letters to the creditor, in which she named the cottage as the pledge for her own carter's bond, and told them it was Ilsa's hand that brought the debt-takers to their door. Garet Tunstall has sworn he has no sister.

Nerys Hallam sold Ilsa Tunstall's file to her master, Leland Groat, the man her letters would ruin; then, to leave no first copy, she set fire to the Oathford letter-writer's stall where Ilsa's letters were written, and it burned with every letter in it. Groat has turned Ilsa off his road and named her a thief to every carrier on it, and Nerys has gone east to the Chainmarket.
Haʻahoqo the General is quarrying the old wall-ground above Crownsgate for a new gate-tower; two of the bank houses below have cracked since spring.

Why here (public): the project is flawed. The old imperial bank survey shows the river has undercut the Crownsgate bank; the quarry will bring the bank houses down, and the tower with them in a wet spring.
The general's steward already held a fair copy of Crownsgate's old bank survey, in a Wayhouse hand, before the village asked the Writers for it.
Cyprian Oddie, the surveyor who kept the Edge survey camp's books, walked out of the camp a month ago and has not come back.
No crime: Cyprian left by choice and took the coast road south. A stranger had shown him copies of his own letters about his debts in Saltmarket, and he could not face the camp knowing they were out.
Oriel Fask was at the Hush grove with three other listeners the night Cyprian left; the Watchtower Ash lamp-keeper saw them there.
The survey camp's stores-book lists a payment of three marks 'to N.H., for copies' the month before Cyprian went.
Ermina Cask, barge-widow of Oathford, died at midsummer; her last letter was dictated at the Oathford letter-writer's stall.
Ermina's last letter left the loft to neither child: it asked that Odo Finch keep his place in it as long as he lives.
Both Cask heirs brought the stall a copy of their mother's last letter, the same letter in two different hands; the stall had sent only one copy, to the Lending Wall.

Miller Gaspard Teel's arrears of eleven measures of salt-tithe have vanished from the Writers' copy of the Mount's tithe-roll; the tithe-house counts its tithe in salt now, and Gaspard is the only miller in the Vale not in arrears.
Aurel Vantry altered the line on Nerys Hallam's order: Gaspard bought his own file from her and paid extra to have his arrears 'corrected' in the Writers' copy.
The Wayhouse had already told Tithe-master Cuthbert Rane, for a fee, that the Teel line was wrong; he has been squeezing Gaspard for it since.
The altered page is a fresh copy on the new rag paper only the Wayhouse buys, in a neat copy-house hand.
Tybalt Garrow, keeper of the Gallows Hill relay loft, was found dead at the foot of the loft ladder at dawn.
Falk Medway, Nerys Hallam's runner, pulled the keeper off the loft ladder in the dark, taking him for the apprentice who had been reading the copies before they flew.
Ruan Toft sat at the Crossroads shrine's fire with the pilgrims all that night.
Inquisitor Cassius Roke has taken Esme Harcourt, the Oathford letter-writer, from her stall for keeping a spy's book of the faithful's letters.
Truth: innocent. Esme keeps no copies; the copies were the halls'.

Inquisitor Roke's charge-sheet quotes Esme's customers' letters word for word, from copies bought 'of a Saltmarket dealer', and names the Oathford stall's copying contract with the Wayhouse as the proof that she spies for the halls.
Aurel Vantry has been sent from the Wayhouse to copy the Old Road dig's survey rolls while the Mount preaches against the halls.
Defect: the contract is worth nothing. The copies it covers are already out of the Wayhouse's presses and on Nerys Hallam's shelves.
The stall has sent the Wayhouse a fair copy of every letter it wrote for nineteen years, under a contract sworn before Old Clerk Amabel Sedge.
Duncan Merrow and the carters of the Oathford road will stand with Ilsa Tunstall, who rode with them nine years. Their price: every copy of their letters given back to them.
Garet Tunstall has said before the gate-village that he will burn the copies on the hearth the night before he leaves for Longwall service, at the new moon.
The file is in the Oathford stall's hand, copied for the Lending Wall; it holds every letter Ilsa ever sent home, and one she never sent.

The last sheet of the Tunstall file is a letter Ilsa had the Oathford stall write to the cottage's creditor, offering her own wages against the debt so that the cottage need not be named. She never sent it.
Ilsa and Garet Tunstall, sister and brother, who have not spoken since the copies came.
Cause: a secret that got told. Agna asked Ilsa to pledge the cottage for her carter's bond, years ago, and never told Garet.
Ilsa's letters home tell, in her own words, of the night loads her master Leland Groat runs round the Oathford toll by the reed path, off his tally.
Nerys Hallam sold Ilsa Tunstall's own file to the man it ruins, and Ilsa lost her post and her name on the Oathford road for it.
Nerys kept a copy of Ilsa's file, as she keeps a copy of everything: her stock at the Chainmarket back-shop is every family on the Oathford road.
Cause: deliberately broken (the last move). The stall's back-room presses kept a copy of every letter for the Lending Wall; that is what burned.
For nineteen years the Oathford stall copied every letter it wrote into its back-room presses, for the Wayhouse.

Benedek Sallow, the Company's own contract-broker at Southroad, has been in the pay of Lord Evander Quillon, the Throne's Recruiter, for two springs. Through caravan houses, bridge-wardens and lesser lords who front for him, Sallow has placed eleven chapter contracts paid in new crown silver and sealed with his own plain brass ring, notched at the rim. Every one posts a Lantern chapter to a bridge, ford or road fort on the Free Lords' border, and binds it there until the Feast of Banners, when the Throne calls its levy. Quillon means the Company to be standing, sworn and unable to leave, wherever the emperor's levy will need it: the Company has been becoming the emperor's army without knowing. When Pell Hartigan matched the notched seal across the boards, Sallow killed him on the Broken Shrine road, taking him for Marthe Grisdale, whose grey and whose satchel Pell was riding. If it comes out, the eleven chapters on those posts pay first: the Free Lords will treat every Lantern on their border as a crown soldier.

At Lord Evander Quillon's petition, the Throne's court at Highcrossing has proclaimed under the old Road Law that every contract paid in crown silver is a crown contract. The eleven Lantern chapters holding them are entered on the crown muster roll, and no quartermaster may end those contracts before the Feast of Banners.

Lord Evander Quillon paid off Sergeant Tamas Grisdale's debts at the Chainmarket and gave him a crown sergeant's commission on the muster roll. Tamas has signed his half of the Longwall chapter onto the levy, and at the Southroad contract board, before the whole inn, he took his mother Marthe Grisdale's lamp down from the board and told her she had shamed the Company by calling its contracts bought.

On the Feast of Banners the Throne's war writ named the Lantern Company: every chapter on the crown muster roll is to march against the Free Lords of the Marches. The Brennock road-fort chapter refused. Lord Evander Quillon told Lamawina that unless she opened Lanternhall to his muster-men, the list of every crown-bought contract on the Free Lords' border would go to the lords of Breakwall and the Chainmarket. She opened the gate. His men now hold the Brennock chapter in Lanternhall's own yard as levy-refusers, and Marthe Grisdale is among the Lanterns pleading for them at the yard rail.
The Longwall chapter's contract to hold the Crownsgate toll bridge runs 'until the Feast of Banners', and not a day past it.
The Brennock road fort's new season contract, posted on the Tally Inn board, is sealed in plain brass with a notch in the rim, and binds the fort's chapter to its walls.
In Pell Hartigan's purse were three crown silver marks of this spring's Highcrossing striking, bright as new.

Both contracts are lawful. Ysabel Brisk's saddles are honest goods, bought and paid for. The Crownsgate bridge-warden's contract to stop war goods bound for the Marches was lawfully posted, and lawfully taken by the Longwall chapter.
Edwy Tarrant will not take saddles that a chapter holding a crown bridge tried to stop: Breakwall cannot be seen arming against the crown.
Gorm Hatchet's Sedge riders took Tansy Quarry off the Brennock road on market eve.

Why taken: to silence her. Tansy kept Gilles Harwood's books, and saw Gorm Hatchet's riders bring him the wool they had taken off his rivals' carts. Gorm took her to keep her from the Chainmarket magistrate, and Harwood wants her back for the same reason.
Pell Hartigan, a Lantern rider out of Southroad, was found dead at the Broken Shrine with his neck broken and his horse grazing beside him.

Benedek Sallow killed Pell Hartigan at the Broken Shrine and took his roll-book. He took the rider on Marthe Grisdale's grey, with her satchel, for Marthe herself, who had been asking the boards about a notched brass seal. Motive: cover-up.
Brother Caddoc was at the Crossroads shrine that night, sitting up with a dying carter; the shrine's keeper saw him there.
Benedek Sallow, Pell Hartigan's old comrade, sold the Company's contracts to the Throne's Recruiter and killed Pell to hide it.
Benedek Sallow left Southroad the night after Pell Hartigan was buried, and now keeps the crown muster pay-office at Highcrossing, which pays every chapter holding a crown-silver contract.
By the Lamp Room's first rule, the quartermaster may put out the lamp of a contract made in a false name: the contract ends, and no Lantern who held it is shamed.

Source: carried in by travellers. The levy company Lord Quillon marched to Crownsgate to count the bridge chapter onto the crown roll came from the Highcrossing levy camp with camp fever; it lies in the levy tents above the bridge camp's well.
Benedek Sallow, now the crown's muster-paymaster, sits at the pay-tent above the Crownsgate bridge and pays the bridge chapter its contract money as 'crown wages', less the levy's keep.
Lord Adrian Hawksmoor of Breakwall has offered the Company his surgeons and his roads for as long as no Lantern rides in a crown levy.
The Crownsgate bridge chapter has been paid a third of its season's contract money, in crown scrip, at Benedek Sallow's pay-tent.

The client's coin came to Sallow in full. He paid it into the levy chest as 'crown wages less keep' and gave the men a third. The Road Law lets the crown pay a crown contract as it likes, so no court will hear it.

Nell Braddock would bring the bridge chapter's lamps to stand with Marthe Grisdale, who vouched for her at the Southroad board twenty years ago. Her price: Lanternhall makes good the season's money Sallow paid into the levy chest.

Nell Braddock carries word between the chapters on the crown roll: the three Marches chapters, Brennock, Breakwall and the Chainmarket, have sworn to each other to stand apart from any levy against the lords whose roads they keep, even if that means standing apart from Lanternhall.
Old Aldous Grisdale, keeper of the Owl Cross lamp for forty years, died at harvest.
Aldous gave his word before two lamp-grave veterans that the lamp-house goes to the elder line, which is Tamas. He never wrote it down. Bryn has kept the lamp and the house with him these ten years.
Tamas Grisdale means to sign the Owl Cross lamp-house over to the crown muster as a levy post on the Feast of Banners, the morning his half-company marches.
Cause: a side taken in someone else's quarrel. Tamas took the crown's side in its quarrel with the Free Lords when his mother would not; neither of them did the other a wrong.
Quillon's price for the commission was that Tamas disown his mother before the board: if Tamas mends it before the march, the muster-men will put his half-company in the levy's van into the Marches.
By the Road Law's water-walk, crown muster-men walk the men they hold to the nearest well at dawn, two guards to a file; Tamas Grisdale has stood that watch at the Longwall muster.
The week before the Feast of Banners, Marthe Grisdale rode to Brennock road fort and sat until midnight with its captain, Moira Stavely.
Honorable: the Brennock chapter refused the war writ to the crown's face and laid down its arms at Lanternhall's gate; it struck no blow.
Marthe Grisdale told Moira Stavely to refuse the writ, and promised her the Company would stand behind her. Marthe's counsel put the Brennock chapter in Quillon's hands.
Sixteen winters ago Kitim Duel-ender killed Oswin Garde on blood terms at the Four Ways stone.

Dav Brook, who fights on the Society's ladder out of the Longwall Gate Yard, is Ambrose Garde, younger brother of Oswin Garde, whom Kitim Duel-ender killed on blood terms at the Four Ways stone sixteen winters ago. He joined the Society under that name. With his yard-master Jessop Mabry booking his bouts and placing his wagers, he has thrown every bout that would lift him off the ninth rung, and bought sponsors to knock off the autumn ladders any climber who could take it from him: the ninth rung, the rung the Firstfrost draw sets against the Duel-ender's exhibition, so that he can meet her on the Ring's sand and kill her there. If it comes out, Edric Garde pays first: Oswin's son, who fights on the same ladder, will be called a Garde plant and struck off with his uncle.

Ambrose Garde, under his own name now, has called his kin home: the Gardes have shut the Gate Yard at Longwall to the Society, chalked over its ring, and turned out the Longwall fighters who boarded there. They swear no Society bout will be fought in Longwall until Kitim Duel-ender answers for Oswin Garde.

On the last night of the autumn circuit the Four Ways stone-house burned with the circuit's bout cards in it. Ambrose Garde came out of the smoke with a tin of wager slips in Wenna Garde's hand, every one betting against her own son. The slips went hand to hand down the bucket line, and before the whole circuit crowd Liʻo of the Ring has struck her from the Ring's chalk and barred her from every ring and circuit stop of the Society as a fixer of bouts.

On Firstfrost eve, Kitim's duel with Oswin Garde was chalked on every challenge stone from the Four Ways to the Ring's gate: 'Kitim Duel-ender killed Oswin Garde and paid nothing.' Before the whole harbour, Ambrose Garde has called her out on blood terms in the Ring at the Firstfrost bouts, for the name Duel-ender.
The Lamb's Yard ladder board has listed 'Dav Brook, Longwall Gate Yard' on the ninth rung for three seasons running.
Before every bout at the Ring, Wenna Garde ties a strip of undyed linen to the east post, for a man who died at the Four Ways stone.
Hettie Coombe paid Nessa Rowntree's entry from a Gate Yard bout-purse, its string tied in three knots and a loop.
At nineteen, Gerrit Vance killed Henner Bly in a tavern duel at Longwall, over a dice-throw.
Gerrit Vance and Cassia Merrow swore under Society rules, before Bel Ashgrove, to a yield bout for Gerrit's place on the fifth rung.
Gerrit Vance holds the fifth rung of the Lamb's Yard ladder.
At the Seamen's shrine last spring, Jago Tremaine swore to open Ros Penhale's head if her lighter tied up at the Long Mole again.
No grant gives the Long Mole berth to either family. The Tremaines tied up there longer; the Penhales more often since the Tremaine lighter sank.
The Carter's Rest autumn ladder's purse is twenty silver, enough to clear the Rowntrees' cart note.

Hettie Coombe owes Jessop Mabry her house. He told her to buy a fighter who could knock Tobyn Reece off the autumn climb, because Tobyn is the one climber who would take the ninth rung from Dav Brook before Firstfrost.
Abe Rowntree promised Nessa that if she won she could keep the purse and go to the Ring at Openharbour; the purse is already promised to the Rowntrees' note-holder.
Edric Garde and Dav Brook swore before Hebe Tansley that a yield bout on the Gull Yard's sand decides the ninth rung.
The ninth rung of the Society's ladder is the one the Firstfrost draw sets against the Duel-ender's exhibition.
For fifteen years Liʻo of the Ring has sold chalk-prints of the Four Ways duel at the Ring's gate, billed as 'the bout that ended dueling'.
When the Gate Yard shut, Ruford Garde wrote up the Longwall fighters' board at three times what they had been paying, and holds young Pim Ashworth at Garde Farm until his is paid.
Inflated: the board was a silver a month for ten years; Ruford's bill charges three, back to midsummer. Mab Hollins, who kept the board book's tallies, can show it.

Ruford Garde says the yard will strike every Longwall fighter's board if the Society meets the Gate Yard in a sworn first-touch bout at the Longwall fair-field, for the Society's right to fight in the Gate Yard.

Sorrel Quist for the Society's Longwall ring and Ambrose Garde for the Gate Yard swore before Godric Fenn to a first-touch bout at the Longwall fair-field: if the Society wins, it may fight in the Gate Yard again.
The Society's right to fight in the Gate Yard ring.

Rowan Garde has bought the touch-judge, Wil Sparrow, to call the bout at the first touch, whoever touches, because Ambrose has told the Gate Yard he will break the Society champion's sword-arm in the second pass. The fix protects Rook Allard.

Rowan Garde says the Gate Yard fights under one relic: the bout card of the Four Ways duel in Oswin's own hand, which Ambrose brought home last winter and Isaut Garde keeps above the hearth at Garde Farm.
Sorrel Quist says the Longwall fighters have asked Kitim to teach again the dawn class she gave up after the Four Ways stone, the killing guards, so that Society fighters can answer real steel.
Last winter the Four Ways bout card was taken from its frame by the Ring's gate; the Ring never learned who took it.

Ambrose Garde, fighting as Dav Brook, took the bout card from the Ring's gate and gave it to his mother as Oswin's last writing. In Oswin's own hand it shows that he chose blood terms. Isaut has it in good faith and paid nothing for it.

Hesketh Bray, the Longwall ladder-keeper who stood as Oswin's second at the Four Ways stone, would stand with Wenna Garde and swear to what Oswin chose that day. His price: the Ring takes in the Longwall fighters, board and floor, until the Gate Yard opens again.

Jessop Mabry set the stone-house fire on Ambrose's word, to break the woman who named him at the Gull Yard and the one second whose face would shame his challenge, and wrote the slips himself, in a hand he learned from the Ring's chalk accounts. He is Ada Mabry's brother.
Col Pritchard's dog woke the stone-house, and he carried Ada's lamp-boy out; the burns on his hands are from the door.
The one bout card that came out of the fire whole is Edric Garde's: he is drawn to fight on the Ring's sand on Firstfrost eve, and his mother is barred from the rail.
Waarua of the Harbour has told Liʻo that if blood is spilled on the Ring's sand, the Open Council takes back the Ring's lease, and the Society goes back to the tavern yards it started in.
Thornwick's fair-ring is a circuit stop: if Osk Penrose lets a barred fixer through, Thornwick loses its place on the Society's circuit and the fair money that comes with it.
Kitim has asked Wenna Garde, of all people, to stand as her second if the Garde challenge comes: the one second nobody could call a killer's friend.
Kitim took up Ambrose Garde's chalk at the Ring's gate, and both swore before Waarua of the Harbour to abide by a blood bout on the Ring's sand.
Kitim's name, Duel-ender.

Ambrose is fighting for his mother as much as for himself: Isaut Garde has kept Oswin's chair empty at the Gate Yard table for sixteen years, and he swore to her she would not die before the name was answered.

Barnaby Quell keeps Dacey Stott in the Wall Steps cellar copy-room, working off a board-and-lamp-oil bill of nine crowns entered in his name, and says he'll sell the boy's indenture at the quarter-day hiring if it isn't paid.

Misassigned: the bill is Ignatius Rawle's. The lodging book shows the scholar's board entered in his own hand all spring; Quell struck the name through and wrote the boy's under it the morning after Rawle took the south road.
Hollin Brede is said to have run from the Ashford road fight eight years ago and left the caravan's lamp in the ditch; the chapter put his lamp out and no client will sign him.

Exaggerated: Brede did leave the fight, but with a boy rider, Desmond Vray, across his saddle, an arrow in the boy's thigh; he rode him to the Crownsgate herb-woman and was back on the road by dawn. The tale grew in the chapter's taproom, retold carelessly, until he had run at the first arrow.
By the Lamb's Yard ladder rule, a fighter who leaves before his rung's bout forfeits his board-bond, and his signed second owes it to the yard.
Caspar has been offered a paid place as the Lamb's Yard's sparring man from spring; going home means losing it, and his father knows, and has told no one at Crownsgate.
Mireille Daunt lies in the loft over the Highcrossing card game with the river sweats; the parish shrine's warden has sworn the lane will be shut and searched by the city watch within the week.
Headman Gregor Plaice has barred the Nettlebank road to anyone carrying the sweats out of the city.
Mireille's fever broke two nights ago; the sweats don't pass once the fever's broken, but nobody at Nettlebank will believe a Night Market fence who says so.

A blank patent of appointment, already under the crown's wax, went missing from the Sealing Room's press-cupboard; Nolan Tusk the wax-scraper is blamed and will be flogged and turned out at the week's end unless he is cleared.

For six years Nolan Tusk has sold the Sealing Room's spoiled wax and the cut-off blank tails of patents on Candle Row, to students and to anyone who asks; the night of the theft he was at the Row selling them.

Linden Grue, the under-sealer's own son, took the blank patent on a night he kept the late fire and sold it to an office-broker on the Gallery Steps to clear his dice debts. Motive: desperation. Two lesser blanks went the same way on earlier late-fire nights.
Florentin Gage's own patent was sealed the morning before the theft; he had no need of a blank.
On Candle Row and in the Sealing Room Nolan Tusk is 'the man who sold the crown's seals'; no chandler will buy his wax and the Sealing Room won't have him back.

Exaggerated: Nolan never sold a seal or a patent. He did sell the Sealing Room's spoiled wax and the blank tails for six years, and some of those tails, under the crown's wax, went into forged toll passes; two honest carters lost their wagons at the Great Bridge when the passes they'd been sold were found out.

When the Tarn's plinth was cleared in the Empty Gallery, the Tarn Foot's colours that hung beside it were taken into the undercroft and put under the Keeper's seal until a ruling on whether a disbanded regiment's colours belong to the Throne or to its last men. No hearing has been called in nine years.
Ensign Rowland Fairlie, Maddox Fairlie's father, carried the Tarn Foot's colours down from the Tarn when the province was lost.

The ruling was never called because the Keeper's ledger lists the colours as crown property, a clerk's error from the day they came in; a hearing would have to correct the Throne's own ledger, and no one has wanted to be the one to ask.

Alaric Fenwright, Weighmaster of the Wool Stair, died at harvest; the office has gone uncle to nephew and father to son for five generations, and his nephew Corvus Lane apprenticed at his scales as a boy.
A Highcrossing office patent must be resealed in a living name by the quarter-day after its holder's death, or it lapses to the crown, which sells lapsed offices to the brokers.
Alaric told Bertram Tibbet in his last week that he wanted the weighing to stay with Felicity for her life and the patent to pass to Corvus after; he never had it written.

Cosmo Varrow kept the wager-bank for the Highcrossing tavern-yard bouts until last spring, when he declared it broke; the season's stakes and the yards' beer-money he held went with it, Saffi Vance's among them. That summer he bought the Saddlers' Row maltings outright.
Wager-stakes are not lawful debts in Highcrossing; no court will hear a claim on a broken wager-bank.
The bank was never broke: Varrow paid out the yards' bettors short for two seasons and kept the difference, then closed it when the books could no longer be squared; the maltings were bought with it.

Philippa Larch for the Upper Stair and Ragna Holloway for the Lower Stair swore before Warden Hugo Merrin that the Midwinter Swim across the crossing decides which crew holds the night-ferry right for the year.
Winifred Cray has paid Simeon Coldry, the starter-judge, to call Aldric for a false start the moment he goes in; Philippa knows it and believes it's for the Lower Stair's sake.
Winifred bought the judge to keep Aldric out of the winter current under the Stair's third pier, the current that took her son, his father, in the same swim; she has said so to no one.

Last autumn Lord Peregrine Ashdale's riders met Idony Marle's free company at Whitlow Ford over a grain convoy; Idony was taken, and Ashdale holds her honourably at his Highcrossing house against a ransom her company can't raise.

Broke quarter: at Whitlow Ford Idony Marle killed two of Ashdale's men after they had thrown down their spears. Ashdale knows; he has set the ransom where it is so that she will stand before the Throne's court instead.

For eleven years Lambert Quine took lamp-club dues from the Longwall chapter's Lanterns and their wives, promising each dead member a lamp kept lit at a lamp grave and a burial; this spring three died and the chest was empty. Quine has set up as a chandler at Crownsgate.

The lamp club was never a lawful club: Quine never registered it with the chapter, so it owes nothing in law; he has been lending its dues at interest to the Crownsgate carters and keeps the notes in his shop.

Each spring the Longwall drill-master holds the Proving: an open trial at arms in the drill yard under the Ninth Tower. Entry needs a sponsor's token from a soldier of rank, and the first three win places in the garrison's guard company, with a soldier's pay.
The Ashfell family owes the Longwall charcoal-master a season's burning; a guard company's pay would clear it in a year.
Haʻahoqo the General has sponsored Proving entrants himself these three springs, and asks each one he sponsors to swear their sword to him by name, as the generals of the old wars did.
Provost Ingram Teller holds the recruit Emeric Sallis in the gatehouse cells, charged with taking the second company's drill-silver from its box on his watch.
Innocent: the drill-silver box was short before Emeric ever stood the watch; the paymaster's own tally, taken the night before, shows it.
Emeric Sallis's sergeant beats the second company's recruits; in the provost's cells Emeric is out of his reach, and he has told his sister he won't come out.
Strangles is in the Wallfoot yards: six dray horses dead since the turn of the month, and the garrison's remounts are stabled across the lane.

Source: a sick animal traded in. Lucius Brand's autumn string came up from the south with two horses already running at the nose; he sold them cheap on the Wallfoot and keeps the rest of the string on the drove field, where the yards water their horses at his trough.
When the Great Bridge was finished, Shahayuh of the South Road sealed a roll naming every family whose man died building it: they cross his bridge toll-free for ever.
Eight years ago Crispin Dole, the masons' guild clerk, took the free-passage roll from the guild chest and sold it for drink; he died the next winter.
Without the roll to show, Shahayuh's toll-reeves have begun charging the masons' widows' carts at the Great Bridge like anyone else's.
Fulke Tremlow bought the roll in a lot of old papers at a Southroad house-sale and framed it over his bar for the lord's seal; he has never read the names.
When the surveyor Evrard Marchant died at Southroad, his effects were sold to pay his lodging; the Lathey coper bought the lot, field journal and all.
Gudrun Lathey's husband kept his last season's horse tallies on the blank backs of the surveyor's journal; she won't part with the last thing he wrote.
The journal's South Road leaves record the old drove ways round every toll between Southroad and the coast; Gudrun has never read past her husband's tallies, and does not know what else is in it.
Josiah Penrick, who kept the Lesser Gate toll-booth forty years, died in the summer; the booth's toll-farm was sealed to him and 'the heirs of his body'.
The lease is plain: the farm goes to Reynard as the heir of the body. Josiah meant Bessamy to keep the booth, said so to Hilde Copse in his last week, and never had it written.
Two weeks ago the iron cramps of the Great Bridge's third pier were found drawn in the night, and a stone dropped into the river.
Captain Roderick Slade has been asking at the carters' lofts for 'the tally-girl with the burned hand' who keeps the night tally at the toll-house.
From the toll-house window Mina Corrow saw two of Lord Varian Ostrey's riders, under Captain Slade, draw the cramps of the third pier with a mason's bar, and knew Slade's face.
Reeve Osric Fenby holds the barge-hand Lowen Brigg in the toll-house lock-up on the Great Bridge, charged with striking the third pier with his barge and loosening its stone.

Innocent: the pier was loosened by Lord Varian Ostrey's riders with a mason's bar, as the night tally-girl saw; Lowen's barge was moored slack on a long line and never touched the stone. The reeve needed a culprit before Shahayuh came home.

Leofric Starling holds Perkin Drewett at the Ninefold Yard, working off the carting bond his father Hodge Drewett owed when he died; by the old bond's terms, if the son walks off, the debt falls on his mother.
Paid: Hodge Drewett paid the last of the bond with his cart and mare the week before he died; Starling took them and never struck the bond. Old Gaddy Pruitt held the mare's head while it was done.

Conal Fisk came up from Saltmarket with his cousin to buy mule teams at the Southroad horse fair after the crews' teams were taken, carrying the crews' purse; three days ago he walked out of the fair at dusk and hasn't been seen since.
The fair-reeve has the drover-boy Wilkin Reave in the stocks for Conal Fisk's disappearance, because he was seen leading a man's horse off the fair at dusk; he'll be whipped off the fair at its end.

Morcant Fisk took the crews' purse from his cousin's saddle-roll on the drove path, and when Conal caught him at it, struck him down and left him in the ditch; Conal lies fevered in a drover's hut a mile down the Bogford road, alive. Motive: desperation; Morcant owes at the Saltmarket quay.
Joachim Thrush was crying his mules at the fair-reeve's post until dark; the reeve's own clerk wrote his last sale.
The horse Wilkin Reave led off the fair was his master's, and his master says so.

Aubrey Kettering said in the Southroad salt market that a Ṭaḍoro-born lord had no business cutting his name in the stones of a Great House bridge; Shahayuh took his clerk's post and banned him from the South Road's toll-roads, and any house on them that shelters him pays the lord's fine.
Mabel's husband has been told by the Oathford lord's bailiff that his eel-lease goes if a banned man is taken into the house; Mabel hasn't told her brother.
Sigeric Haw, boat-master of the toll-chain, pressed Benet Marsh off the eel-smokers' row onto the lord's chain-boats for the winter, without wages, under the river-bailiff's press-warrant.

Lord Aymer Rothwell ordered the boat-master to fill the chain-boats from the smokehouse row, because the row has no lord to complain to; the warrant covers vagrants, not a man with a trade, and the bailiff swore it anyway.
Twice a year, at the spring and autumn readings, the archive reads the year's new lines aloud from the stair of the Ninth Ring's sunken court; the whole town crowds the court to hear them.

This winter Lord Gerent Penmarrow bought the Ashcombe house-debt and called it in two seasons before its term. The Ashcombes lost the third-ring rooms their house had held for nine generations, and the Penmarrows' younger son lives in them now.

Lord Gerent needed the rooms by midsummer: his younger son's betrothal into an inner house was promised on his holding third-ring rooms by then. The Ashcombe debt's own terms ran to the harvest after next, and Gerent's mother, who keeps the house-purse, was never told how the rooms were got.

Lady Celandine Thornbury's stone-tenders are feeding a new low wing onto the Thornbury house, on its own garden ground beside Copyists' Row: the house's old doors have grown too high for her mother to use.
Project sound: the Thornbury wing will grow as its stone-tenders plan and stand for generations. Its footings spread under Copyists' Row as it grows, lifting the row's floors and splitting its walls.

Mardoc Lusk's band took two Lantern riders, Idony Selk and Wendel Harrow, off the Firststone road with the Varrow house's carts, and holds them at the old ring-quarry for ransom. Haldane Strick, who hired them, has refused to pay.

Why the client won't pay: the contract was cover. Haldane Strick hired the riders to escort 'the Varrow house's winter wool' to Ashring; the carts were carrying the Varrow house's gifts to the True Line at Firststone, which the Varrows' Seated House patrons must never learn of. Paying the ransom would mean saying what the carts carried.
At the autumn reading, in the crush on the sunken court's stair, a house-guard fell and broke his arm; Warden Osgood Prynne took Hamo Ash for striking him, and holds him in the cells under the court.
Innocent: the guard missed his footing on the wet stair and took Hamo down with him; half the water-carriers on the stair saw it, and none of them will say so to a ring-warden unasked.

Last autumn Tobias Wren, head of the Wren house of the sixth ring, sold the Merrow family, Open Hand wool traders, a place in the Wren line: the archive now lists the Merrows as Wren cousins, and his sister Damaris's children share their house-name with strangers.

Tobias sold the line to pay his debt to Clerk-master Ambrus Fell, who entered the Merrows in the lesser rolls himself and took the debt out of the price. Tobias kept nothing: the Wren house was already ruined, and he has told no one, least of all Damaris.

Since the Corvell bridge's handrail gave way at midwinter and a guest of the house fell, the Corvell steward has stopped Joram Peck's wage and bread, saying he broke his indenture; Joram has stopped tending the bridge, saying the house broke it first.

The indenture binds the house to send rope and timber each autumn and the keeper to tell the steward when the bridge needs them. Joram told the old steward four times; the old steward died in the winter with none of it written down, and the indenture also says the keeper pays for rope 'in want of the house's'.

Master Cadell Rooke sold six outer-ring families grown-stone cuttings at a house's price, to grow them rooms against the ninth ring's wall. Not one cutting has taken in two years, and he says stone takes in its own time.

The cuttings were dead when he sold them: Cadell cuts them from the rubble of fallen eighth-ring houses, where grown stone has died. Lord Warden Percival Hythe, who licenses Cadell's stall in the sunken court, takes a share of every sale and has twice ruled the families' complaint 'a matter of patience'.

Osmund Saltash contracted, in writing, to search the archive for Merel Dunning's descent for a fee in five payments. She missed the fifth when her mother fell sick. Under the contract he keeps the four payments and the proof he found, until the fifth is paid.

Osmund found Merel's line, and it runs true to a fifth-ring house; but her father's grandmother was a Horaro of the Reef. He has said nothing of it to her, and means to sell her the proof at the full price anyway.

Each spring the True Line holds a hill-run at Firststone for the young who would serve its house; a runner must bring a proof of line or a sponsor's word to enter, and the few who finish first are taken into the First-Stone household.
The run's prize: a place in the First-Stone household for the first finishers, with board, and the house's word for their kin.

If Merel enters on the line-finder's proof, it will be read out at the start: her father's grandmother was a Horaro of the Reef, and the True Line turns away any runner whose line is not 'pure'. Ruʻo reads every proof aloud himself.

The east wing and its spring court lie inside the First-Stone House's oldest wall and were never granted or let to the Hollins. They moved in when the wing fell and the house moved out of it, thirty years ago, and have kept the spring clear and the court's roof on ever since.
Steward Fulke Arden has told the Hollins to be out of the east court by the new moon: the house means to lodge this spring's young hopefuls there.

At the midsummer tithe Armsman Garth Ulley struck Davy Rennick, a young drover from the Vale farms, down on the tithe stair below the Armed Nave; Davy died that night. Captain Aldred Mortlake has said his armsman kept the stair as he was told, and no court has heard it.

Davy had already paid his tithe and turned to go down when Garth struck him from behind, for a word Davy said over his shoulder. Tilly Pask, a pilgrim girl from Ashring, saw it; she has kept quiet because the captain holds her brother's tithe-debt.

Garrow Thane's band of deserters from the Armed Nave took Ysolde Brennan, the pilgrim hospice's bonesetter, from the hospice road at dusk; two of the band broke their legs in a fall on the north crag, and they need her to set them.

By an old Elderhollow custom, a family leaving the town may be called out once, in the stump-ring of the vanished house, by any man who says its going shames the town; the call must be answered before the family goes.

Edmund Kestrel has called Piran Treve out in the stump-ring on blood terms, before the Treves leave Elderhollow, saying a Horaro house that walks away from the Alliance shames the town that kept it; before the reeve, as the custom requires, both have sworn to abide by the bout.
By the stump-ring custom, a called man who will not fight, or who yields, takes his family out of Elderhollow struck from the town roll, as if the house had never been there.

Edmund has nothing against Piran. The Elderhollow house guard takes one new man a year, and a blood win in the stump-ring is the old way to be noticed; Piran is simply the only leaving man who cannot refuse the call.

The Change-Yard Writ, from the Open Council's first year, lets any crew change teams in the Carter's Rest change-yard without fee, for as long as the yard's keeper holds it; it hangs framed behind the Harness Inn's bar.

Thirty years ago Ewart Bascombe, then the Road Crews' yard-clerk, took the Change-Yard Writ from the crews' strongbox and pawned it; Widow Hilde Tullis's late husband bought it with the Harness Inn at the pawn sale, not knowing where it came from.
Silvan Coote is buying the writ for a carting house that means to keep it in a strongbox and charge the change-yard's fee itself; he has told Widow Hilde it is for a collector of Council papers.

Forty years ago Seraphine Marlowe's grandfather sold the Marlowe house-book to Quentin Amblin's father for the price of a winter's bread; it has stood in the Amblin book-room ever since, and Quentin will not sell it at any price.

The Marlowe house-book records that the house's founder, five generations back, was a bond-servant bought from a Great House lord and freed in the Ninth Ring, and took the Marlowe name when he was. It is the only record of it: the archive's own entry for the Marlowes was copied from the book, and the copyist left that page out.
Osgood Varrow, a Bogford-born digger who worked his own bog-iron claim on the Breakwall bog, died at midwinter and left no word on who should have it.
