By Kotqot Wall-breaker's rule for the Breakwall bog, as for his breach, a claim belongs to whoever can hold it: one that no one works through the thaw goes back to the keep.
Fulke Varrow took an advance from the Breakwall smith Hedwig Stannard against the first season's ore from his brother's claim, and has spent it.
Isaura Varrow worked the claim's wash-trough beside her father for the last three winters and nursed him at the end; Fulke had not set foot on the bog in four years.

The claim is buried in debt: two winters ago Osgood bought the work-time of four bonded diggers from the Breakwall debt-broker against the claim itself, and the debt that falls due at the thaw is more than a season of ore.

Lambert Ashgrove and Radulf Stour swore before the market-reeve Gisla Brenhold that the spring chain-carry, the old harbour chain borne round the Chain Walk, would decide whose gang holds the Block's portering right for the year.
Melisande Dray has bought the Chain Walk's line-judge, Nib Calder, to call the Low Gate gang's chain down at the last turn.

Lambert Ashgrove has promised Yann Coldridge his bond-paper if the Low Gate gang wins the chain-carry; but a month ago Lambert sold Yann's bond, and his sister Elske's with it, to Hamund Grice of the Breakwall bog-iron pits, who takes them both at month's end whoever wins.
A Breakwall pit-boss, Hamund Grice, has taken a room at the Tally Inn for the week after the chain-carry.
Yann Coldridge ran from Hamund Grice's bog-iron pits at Breakwall on the night of the dawn count, and Grice's tally-men are walking the bog for him.
Hamund Grice bought Yann's and Elske's bonds as a pair, on the term that if one runs the pair's whole price falls on the one who stays: Elske's years double the morning Yann is gone.
The breach in Breakwall's outer wall stands open day and night by Kotqot's rule, and the drove-road to the Last Wave's Proving Ground runs out through it.

Three winters ago Osbert Fallow, Kotqot Wall-breaker's timber-master, had the sawyer Aelred Mott turned off the keep's saw-pit and branded a timber-thief, for a raft of the lord's oak that went missing on the bog river.
Osbert Fallow now runs the keep's saw-pit himself, and every family on the Sawyers' Row, Aelred Mott's own, lives on its work.
Kotqot Wall-breaker will hear no word against the timber-master who keeps the keep's timber coming.

Osbert Fallow sold the missing raft himself, to a Chainmarket timber-buyer, and cut Aelred's mark into the tally-stick after the raft was gone; the saw-pit's mastership was the price of Aelred's name.
The Ashcombes of the Chainmarket say their great-grandmother bought herself off the Block in its first years, and that it was written down.
Mab Thursby doesn't know what the old ledger under her counter is. Her husband told her that while she kept it no broker would ever touch her, and she has kept it, and wraps nothing in it.

The ledger is the Block's first sale-book, kept by Mab's husband's grandfather, the Block's first clerk: every sale and every self-purchase of its first seven years, the only record left of which Chainmarket families came up off the Block free, and on what terms. The brokers who knew it existed have left her alone.

The Ninemile bell rang captives in for water at a Walking Road waystation until liberators burned it; a tinker carted it to the Chainmarket for its bronze and abandoned it rather than pay the metal-duty.
The market-reeve holds the Ninemile bell in her pound until someone pays the metal-duty owed on it; at the quarter-day it goes to the duty-sale.
Gisla Brenhold wants the bell gone: freed folk come by night to sit at the pound rail beside it, the brokers complain of it to her daily, and she cannot be seen to give up a held pledge.
Sefton Gall's fen band took Wren Vossel off the Coldwater road for her copying hand.
Sefton Gall's band needs a hand that can copy a Chainmarket broker's seal and bond-script.
Effie Ludgate, a free girl Sefton Gall's band took from the fens, is held at the Coldwater sheepfold with Wren, waiting on the bond-paper Wren is being made to write for her.
This season's contract for the Brennock road fort was posted at the Tally Inn board by a Chainmarket caravan house.

Why here (public): opportunity. With the fort's chapter held to its walls by its season contract, the drovers' halt an hour down the road has no one to call, and Rendel Garrow's bog-reivers take the herds and stores the drovers leave there.
The Breakwall Lantern chapter holds Kotqot Wall-breaker's writ to bring Rendel Garrow to the keep's court alive.
By the Free Lords' grant, the Reedbank causeway into the fens is the Binders' road: nothing crosses without the camp's leave, and no iron crosses at all.
Hobb Tennant spent six years' wages at the Breakwall forges on forty bog-iron spearheads, for the free hamlet of Fenholt past the reeds.
The Reedbank camp's keeper sells the raiders' routes, and the gaps between them, to whoever pays.

Duvall Hesk stops iron at the causeway because he knows the Free Lords' standing order: a fen hamlet found with iron is a rebel hamlet, and Breakwall's garrison burns it and the Binders take every soul in it. Unarmed, Fenholt loses a straggler a season to the camp; armed, it loses everyone.
Owyn Pellow is held in the Last Well's chain-shed against his debt to the Chainmarket broker Saul Marten, to be walked to the Block at the next market.
Families leave tokens at the Last Well for the ones who were taken; Maudie Pellow has hung Owyn's eel-hook there.
Inflated: Crispin Wardle has entered keep and water against Owyn at every waystation on the Walking Road, though Owyn never passed through one; the debt now stands at three times what he borrowed.
Owes the captor: all season Crispin Wardle has let Maudie bring Owyn bread on credit at the Last Well, and he has told her what he will take for it if she crosses him.

Thirty years ago, when the Starling house on Reefhold's outer stilts was pulled down for debt, the stilt-breaker Gorlan Grey carried off its carved line-post and sold it, though by custom a house's line-post goes to its family.

Gorlan Grey sold the post to Barnaby Quell's father for timber, swearing the Starlings had sold it to him. Under the tar it is carved with six generations of Starling divers; it carries the ridge of the net-loft, and Barnaby has never known whose names are on it.
The Speaker's Deck is built to sink a hand's width a year, so that every generation must rebuild it.
The new season's speaker takes the Speaker's Deck at the turning of the tide-season, and at high water the deck now stands a forearm under the lagoon.
No long timber is left on the Reef Coast: the stand that gave the old Deck its long piles was cut out two generations ago.

Cause: built badly. To save long timber, Halloran Deake set the new Deck on short piles bound with kelp-rope; the lagoon mud takes short piles four times as fast, and the deck meant to sink a hand a year has sunk a forearm in twelve.
Flux has gone through Reefhold's poor stilts this month: eleven are down, the youngest worst.
The back stilts buy their water from Jago Bream's shore cistern-house; the clean cistern on the front walks will not sell to them.

Source: bad water. The spring tides cracked the lining of Jago Bream's cistern and it has drawn brackish seep since; Jago knows the taste has turned and has kept selling, because there is nothing else for the back stilts to buy.
Sorcha Tregear, a kelp diver, was found drowned at the outer kelp-ropes with her dive-rope parted.
The back stilts say Kenver Sloane drowned his wife after their quarrel on the walk the night before; his own crew won't dive with him.
The Binders have offered a price for the names of runaway bondsmen sheltered by the Far Sails.
Kenver Sloane was at the kelp-boil on the far point from dusk to dawn the night Sorcha drowned; twenty cutters saw him there.

Daveth Kitto cut Sorcha's rope at the outer kelp-ropes. Two days before, she had paid the letter-writer to write to a Binder factor at the Chainmarket, offering the names of the runaways Daveth rows out to the Far Sails at night, for the Binders' price; Daveth drowned her to keep the names from leaving the reef. Motive: preservation.
Lucius Corder, the Throne's furs-tax collector, has sat at the High Snows' Guest Fire since last thaw. He is sacred while he sits; the clans keep the stair below it.
Bjarne Whitlock guided Lucius Corder's party up the Gap trail last thaw.
The Great House sends a tax collector up to the High Snows every few years. He never comes back down, and no one asks why.

Broke quarter: at the foot of the snow stair, when the clansmen who barred the furs-tax laid down their spears, Lucius Corder ordered his escort to cut them down, and three died. He reached the Guest Fire ahead of the clans' answer and has not stood up since.
At the summit of Textrim's Height the priestesses' fire has never been let go out.

Totkit Sea-crosser keeps a striped hunting cat brought over the sea from the old country, the last of its kind on the island, in a walled run on the ridge between the Proving Ground and the lower steps. Harming it is an offence against the war-chief.
The run's wall came down in the autumn rains at its gully corner; Druth Mallon has been propping it with brush instead of reporting it, because the war-chief would have his place for it.

Why here: opportunity. Since the young warriors went down to the Proving Ground, the charcoal-burners' huts on the outer slope stand outside the walls with no one to guard them, and a Binder band has twice taken children out gathering wood.
In the autumn Gudrun Holk agreed with Emeric Sallow, before the lower-gate tally-keeper, to forge forty blades for sixty sacks of lowland barley, the barley first.
The middle sacks of the barley took the wet on the river road: under the top layers it is sprouting and black, and half of it won't keep to midwinter.

Both sides broke it: Emeric's sacks came in under weight (the tally-keeper counted the sacks, not the weight), and Gudrun has held back ten of the forty blades for her own kin's spears. Neither knows how little the barley is worth.
Nine winters ago the salt forges' roof came down in a fire; Sigurd Ostery died under it, and his widow Imra Coldwell named the forge-master, Fenrik Aske, as the man who had overloaded the beams.

No line was ever drawn through the Black Stand: the fire-keepers took the windfall and the forges the standing wood, by habit, until this winter's hunger sent the households in after both. The beams that killed Sigurd were green pine from the Stand, cut in a hurry because the fire-keepers had claimed the seasoned wood that year.
Piet Hallam sold the Fell forge's salt-folding, the way its blades are folded with forge salt, to a lowland smithy at Bogford for a winter's grain money, which he sent to his own kin below the Rim.

Ondra knew. Piet sold the folding with her leave, because her own forge-kin had cut the two of them out of the enclave's grain share for the marriage, and the money fed his mother's house through the autumn.

Last winter Radulf Brede stood in the Circle against Kettil Brune and was let in to speak; there he hired Ravna Stoke's band to guard his winter droves on the Rim road, the pay to be grain and the band's winter quarters in his paddock-house below the Circle.

The deal sworn in the Circle was for the droves on the road only; the forty head lost were taken from the paddock folds, which Ravna's band were never paid to guard. Radulf withheld the grain for losses the band were never sworn to.
Yrsa Kettle's hunting party crossed Ash Gully to the high scree twelve days ago and has not come back; the rope bridge behind them is down, and the camp has been left empty.
Mikkel Aster cut the bridge ropes half through the night after Yrsa turned him off the hunt, meaning only to make her party late back and laughed at at the winter count. He didn't reckon on the snow.
At the Soft Hollow's Listening Trees the sworn press their ears to the bark to hear the dead.
Since the spring a new voice speaks from one of the Listening Trees, and both Elspet Varrow and Nesta Dree say it is the drowned ferryman Evrard Dree.

Before Mother Bryony, Elspet Varrow and Nesta Dree swore to let a long listen decide who keeps the ferryman's tree: from dusk to dawn with an ear to the bark, and the first to speak or sleep gives it up.
Elspet promised Ansgar Rake that if he sat the long listen for her and won, she would go back down to the ford with him and marry him. She means to stay by the tree for good.
Ancel Fenn, a smith of Ashring, walked into the green two winters ago and came to stay at the Soft Hollow; he carried his forge-set in on a hand-cart and gave it at the trees.

The forge-set was Ancel's alone, left to him by his father's will in front of the Ashring headman; Tilde's story that it was her mother's dowry is what her mother told her to keep the house from selling it.
Clemence Lusk of the Writers has measured the green against the Year Cairns from Watchtower Thorn all summer: it is coming on faster than any year cut on the cairns.
Before Hoqa of the Green Wall, Quill Merrow and Orrin Stagg swore by Warden custom that the dusk shoot at Thorn's butts decides who keeps the tower this winter.
Orrin Stagg fletched Quill Merrow's shoot arrows with glue that softens in the evening damp: loaded gear.

Orrin rigged the shoot to keep Quill out of Thorn: from Clemence Lusk's measures he reckons the green will reach the tower before midwinter, and whoever keeps it this winter will not come back to the Wall. He means it to be himself.
Thorn's second keeper, Barnaby Ferrand, hasn't been seen at the tower since the first frost, and its night signal has been dark since.
A Rooted listener sits in the trees over the swallowed cairns and talks softly to anyone who rests there.

Barnaby never deserted: Orrin sent him away from Thorn himself after the cairn readings, so that one man fewer would be in the tower when the green comes, and has kept the night signal dark so the Wall won't count Thorn's men until Barnaby is clear.

The Hush grove was burned out by Wardens from Watchtower Ash in the spring; one Rooted woman stayed in the ashes, and since then the voices there have asked, night after night, for Ruari Heddle by name.
The bead Ruari has worn since he was nine is a seed of the green. His mother gave it to him the night she walked into the trees; planted in the burned ring, it would grow the grove back.
This autumn one of the Open Council hall's old ledger rooms was emptied by whoever holds its key, and its papers were sold off as scrap by the bale on the Salt Steps.

In Lowell Tapper's bale was the First Council's grant giving the freed families of Shackle Row their houses for as long as the Hand stands; he has bound its vellum as the cover of his own shop book. It is the only copy: the Council's register page for it was in the same ledger room.
